content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I made a quick assessment of this paper.
content.review:
This paper explores fast normalization schemes for bilinear pooling in deep neural networks. The scheme basically approximates an SVD through K iterations of the power method, applied to a random vector. The performance is compared, in terms of computational time and accuracy degradation, with max pooling, sum pooling, and other SVD-based normalization schemes in bilinear pooling. 

I am not too familiar with this area, so I cannot speak to whether this idea is novel or whether the practice of bilinear pooling is widely used; however, it seems from the experiment that the idea works well and can greatly increase performance in smaller neural nets (VGG is used) on complex tasks. Additionally, using the power method to approximate an SVD makes sense, and the tests seem fairly extensive. 

One comment is that I find the method seems a bit complicated in description. Why is the expectation subtracted? Why are so many steps needed after the power method is completed? Additionally, the details for the back propagation seems not very relevant to the method idea, and could be moved to the appendix, with just a description on computational complexity in the main text. While I believe that each step was important, I think the motivation behind each step should be emphasized over the mechanics, which are a bit convoluted. 

Otherwise, I think the paper is a nice contribution.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thanks for the reviewer's encouraging comments and the valuable suggestions.
Below we address the  specific questions raised by the reviewer.

Q1: Why conduct subtraction?
A1: We subtract the constructed rank-1 matrix to achieve the goal of normalization on the singular values. 
Please refer to Theorem 1 in the updated manuscript.

Q2: Why are so many steps needed after the power method is completed?
A2: We rewrite the section 3 and summarize the proposed RUN in Algorithm 3. As you can see, we only need one additional step after power method. 

Q3: The details for the back propagation seems not very relevant to the method idea, and could be moved to the appendix.
A3: Thanks for your suggestions.  We have moved the back propagation to the appendix.

content.title: response
content.comment:
Q1 response: I was thinking that in general it would make more sense to re-scale the singular values multiplicatively. But in retrospect that seems not great for GPUs and parallelization, whereas subtraction may work better for that. Is that the logic you're using?

Overall I think the paper reads much better!

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper proposes a rank-1 update normalization (RUN), which supports the normalization on compact bilinear features and feasible to be plugged into end-to-end training. RUN uses power method to estimate the bilinear matrix, which is more friendly to GPU. The idea of RUN is well motivated but not surprising. The experimental results show RUN achieves comparable accuracies with much lower running time than NS iteration and SVD-based normalization. 

The presentation of this paper should be improved. It is necessary to summarize the procedure of RUN like Algorithm 1 and 2. The main results in Section 3 are desired to be presented by Theorem or Proposition. Some detailed derivation could be deferred into appendix.

Some questions:

1. It is unclear how to obtain (16) from previous derivation. Where does \epsilon come from?

2. Can you provide non-asymptotic results of (18) and (21) (which may be rely on the eigengap)? 

3. It would like to plot how the accuracy of each algorithms varying with epochs and running time. 

Minor comments:

1. Should v_i in section 3 be standard normal distribution?

2. In the sentence between (11) and (12): normalization distribution -> normal distribution.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thanks for the reviewer's constructive suggestions for writing. We have rewritten the section 3. We present main results in Section 3  as Theorems and  detailed derivations are moved into appendix. Below we address the specific questions raised by the reviewer.

Q1: how to obtain Eq. (16) ? What is \epsilon?
A: We rewrite section 3 to make it clearer. The Eq. (16) in the previous version is Eq. (5) in the current version. \epsilon is  a small constant \in [0,1]. 

Q2: Can you provide non-asymptotic results of (18) and (21)?
A2:  Since non-asymptotic results of Eq. (18) and (21) in the old version depend on the initialization vector \mathbf{v}_0. Thus, we give their expectations with respect to random initialized vector \mathbf{v}_0 in Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 in the updated manuscript.

Q3: Plot how the accuracy of each algorithms varies in different epochs. 
A3:  We plot the accuracy change of the proposed RUN in different epochs in Appendix C of the updated manuscript.

Q4: Should v_i in section 3 be standard normal distribution?
A4:  We only assume v_0 as standard normal distribution. The standard power method does not require v_0 to be normal distribution. But for easiness of computing the expectation, we sample items in v_0 by standard normal distribution.

Q5: In the sentence between (11) and (12): normalization distribution -> normal distribution.
A5: Thanks for help. We have fixed this typo.

content.title: Response
content.comment: Thanks again for kidingly pointing out the typos and presentation issues. We have uploaded a revised version.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The authors consider a bilinear matrix normalized network and how to implement the bilinear matrix normalization, which uses SVD, in a manner that allows end-to-end training. The key idea used is to use the fact that singular values of a matrix can be found via the power method, which requires repeatedly multiplying a matrix with a vector and normalizing the resulting product.  Experiments are demonstrated on some multi-class datasets of fairly small size. The writing could have been better and i found the exposition somewhat hard to follow. Here are  a few comments and questions.

1. It was hard to follow the RUN procedure. I was able to figure out the use of power method, but it was not clear to me what the key result of Section 3 is? I would suggest that the authors rework the exposition in this section to clearly state what the main result is.

2. The latter half of Section 3 shows the derivatives w.r.t. F. I appreciate the authors working through these calculations, but I do not see why it is important. It was not clear to me what the authors wanted to express via the calculation of the derivative.

3. The datasets used for experimentation are rather small. Why is this the case? What is the limiting factor?

I like the idea of using power iterations and exposing the power iterations as a sequence of layers. However, the exposition needs a lot to be desired.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thanks for the reviewer's constructive suggestions for writing. We rewrite the section 3 and polish the other sections.  We present the main steps and properties in Algorithms and Theorems and move the detailed derivations to the Appendix.   Below we address questions raised by the reviewer:

Q1:  It was hard to follow the RUN procedure. 
A1:  We rewrite the section 3, and summarize the RUN algorithm in Algorithm 3. As you can see, it is quite simple. We apologize for making it difficult to follow in the previous revision.

Q2:  Section 3 shows the derivatives w.r.t. F. but I do not see why it is important.
A2: We derive the derivatives w.r.t. F for reader to better understand the back-probation happens in the proposed method. We agree with the reviewer that, using the autograd tool provided by Pytorch or TensorFlow,   it is unnecessary to manually derive this in practice. Therefore, we move the derivatives calculations to Appendix B.

Q3:  Why the datasets used for experimentation are small?
A3:  The datasets we use are most widely used for evaluating bilinear pooling. Since the compared methods are all evaluated on these datasets and thus we choose these datasets as well.

content.title: Read the rebuttals
content.comment: I have read the authors rebuttals and other reviewers reviews. My opinion has not changed. I think this could be a nice contribution but the presentation needs improvement.

content.title: Response
content.comment: Thanks so much. We have uploaded a new version, please take a look when you get a chance.
